question.text:
Given that $A$ is a $3\times2$ matrix, $B$ is a $2\times5$ matrix, and $C$ is a $5\times3$ matrix, in which of the following expressions are the Hadamard products well-defined?

  1. $AB \odot C$
  2. $AB \odot C^T$
  3. $(AB)^T \odot C$
question.explanation:
The Hadamard product of two matrices (or vectors) is only defined if they have the same dimensions.

Let's consider each expression in turn:

  • The dimensions of $AB$ are $3\times5,$ and the dimensions of $C$ are $5\times3.$ Hence, the Hadamard product in expression I is not well-defined.

  • The dimensions of $AB$ are $3\times5,$ and the dimensions of $C^T$ are $3\times5.$ Hence, the Hadamard product in expression II is well-defined.

  • The dimensions of $(AB)^T$ are $5\times3,$ and the dimensions of $C$ are $5\times3.$ Hence, the Hadamard product in expression III is well-defined.

Therefore, the correct answer is "II and III only".

question.text:
Given that $X$ is a $2\times4$ matrix, $Y$ is a $4\times2$ matrix, and $Z$ is a $4\times4$ matrix, in which of the following expressions are the Hadamard products well-defined?

  1. $XY \odot Z$
  2. $YX \odot Z^T$
  3. $(XY)^T \odot Z$
question.explanation:
The Hadamard product of two matrices (or vectors) is only defined if they have the same dimensions.

Let's consider each expression in turn:

  • The dimensions of $XY$ are $2\times2,$ and the dimensions of $Z$ are $4\times4.$ Hence, the Hadamard product in expression I is not well-defined.

  • The dimensions of $YX$ are $4\times4,$ and the dimensions of $Z^T$ are $4\times4.$ Hence, the Hadamard product in expression II is well-defined.

  • The dimensions of $(XY)^T$ are $2\times2,$ and the dimensions of $Z$ are $4\times4.$ Hence, the Hadamard product in expression III is not well-defined.

Therefore, the correct answer is "II only".

question.text:
\[
A = \begin{bmatrix} 3 & -3 \\ 0 & -2 \end{bmatrix}, \quad
B = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix}, \quad
\mathbf{y} = \begin{bmatrix} 2 \\ -1 \end{bmatrix}.
\]
Given the matrices above, write the following expression as a Hadamard product. Here $(\,\cdot\,)$ denotes matrix multiplication.
question.explanation:
The Hadamard product of two compatible vectors $\mathbf{u}$ and $\mathbf{v}$ can be expressed as the matrix product \[ \mathbf{v} \odot \mathbf{u} = \text{diag}(\mathbf{v})\mathbf{u}. \]

In our case, we have \[ AB = \begin{bmatrix} 3 & -3 \\ 0 & -2 \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 3 & 0 \\ 0 & -2 \end{bmatrix} \] and \[ B\mathbf{y} = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} 2 \\ -1 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 1 \\ -1 \end{bmatrix}. \]

Hence,

\begin{align*} (AB) \cdot (B \mathbf{y}) &= \begin{bmatrix} 3 & 0 \\ 0 & -2 \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} 1 \\ -1 \end{bmatrix}\\[5pt] & =\text{diag}\bigg(\begin{bmatrix} 3 \\ -2 \end{bmatrix} \bigg) \begin{bmatrix} 1 \\ -1 \end{bmatrix}\\[5pt] & = \begin{bmatrix} 3 \\ \bbox[4pt,border: 1px solid lightgray]{-2} \end{bmatrix} \odot \begin{bmatrix} \bbox[4pt,border: 1px solid lightgray]{ 1} \\ \bbox[4pt,border: 1px solid lightgray]{-1} \end{bmatrix} \end{align*}

The Hadamard product of two compatible vectors $\mathbf{u}$ and $\mathbf{v}$ can be expressed as the matrix product \[ \mathbf{v} \odot \mathbf{u} = \text{diag}(\mathbf{v})\mathbf{u}. \]

In our case, we have \[ AB = \begin{bmatrix} -3 & 0 \\ -4 & 4 \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ 1 & 1 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} -3 & 0 \\ 0 & 4 \end{bmatrix} \] and \[ B\mathbf{y} = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ 1 & 1 \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} -1 \\ 3 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} -1 \\ 2 \end{bmatrix}. \]

question.text: Given that \[ P\odot (Q+R) = \begin{bmatrix} 6 & -2 \\ 1 & 3 \end{bmatrix} \quad\text{and}\quad X = \begin{bmatrix} 4 & 0 \\ -5 & 2 \end{bmatrix}, \] find $(Q \odot P+ R \odot P) -X^T.$
question.explanation:
For compatible matrices $A,$ $B,$ and $C,$ and scalar $\alpha,$ the Hadamard product has the following properties:

  • Commutativity: \[ A \odot B = B \odot A \]

  • Associativity: \[ (A \odot B) \odot C = A \odot (B \odot C) \]

  • Distributivity over Addition: \[ A \odot (B + C) = A \odot B + A \odot C \]

  • Scalar Distributivity: \[ \alpha (A \odot B) = (\alpha A) \odot B = A \odot (\alpha B) \]

In this case, by the commutativity of the Hadamard product, we have \[ (Q \odot P+ R \odot P) -X^T= (P \odot Q + P \odot R) -X^T. \]

Then, by the distributivity over the addition of the Hadamard product, we have

\begin{align*} (P \odot Q + P \odot R) -X^T &= P\odot (Q + R) -X^T\\[5pt] &= \begin{bmatrix} 6 & -2 \\ 1 & 3 \end{bmatrix} - \begin{bmatrix} 4 & 0 \\ -5 & 2 \end{bmatrix}^T \\[5pt] &= \begin{bmatrix} 6 & -2 \\ 1 & 3 \end{bmatrix} - \begin{bmatrix} 4 & -5 \\ 0 & 2 \end{bmatrix} \\[5pt] &= \begin{bmatrix} 6-4 & -2-(-5) \\ 1-0 & 3-2 \end{bmatrix} \\[5pt] &= \begin{bmatrix} 2 & 3 \\ 1 & 1 \end{bmatrix}. \end{align*}
